title: Harmony
intro: Harmony is how chords follow one another. In tonal music each chord has a function: tonic (home), predominant (moving away) or dominant (pulling back home). The order tonic, predominant, dominant, tonic describes most phrases from Bach to the Beatles.

items: Tonic (T): I, and its substitutes vi and sometimes iii. Stable; phrases start and end here.
Predominant (PD): IV and ii (also ii7, IV7, and in minor iv, ii°, VI). Leads to the dominant.
Dominant (D): V, V7 and vii°(7). Unstable; contains the leading tone and, in V7, a tritone that resolves to the tonic.

blocks.text: A typical phrase moves T → PD → D → T: I–IV–V–I, I–ii6–V7–I, i–iv–V–i. Going backwards (V to IV) happens, especially in rock, but in common-practice style it weakens the sense of direction.

The strongest progressions move the root down a fifth (up a fourth): V→I, ii→V, vi→ii. Chains of falling fifths, I–IV–vii°–iii–vi–ii–V–I, are the 'circle of fifths' sequence heard in Baroque music and in jazz standards. Roots falling by a third (I–vi–IV–ii) move between chords that share two notes, smoothly. Roots rising by step (IV–V, V–vi) need care in voice leading to avoid parallel fifths.

The rate at which chords change is the harmonic rhythm. It usually speeds up approaching a cadence: one chord per bar for most of a phrase, then two or more per bar into the ending. Chords usually change on strong beats.

To analyse a passage: find the key; identify each chord's root, quality and inversion; label it with a Roman numeral and figure (V6/5, ii6, I6/4). Notes outside the chord are labelled as non-chord tones. The analysis is not just labels: it shows how the phrase moves from tonic through predominant to dominant and back.

items: Voice Leading (#/arts/music-theory/harmony/voice-leading): writing chords in four parts that move well.
Non-Chord Tones (#/arts/music-theory/harmony/non-chord-tones): passing tones, neighbours, suspensions and more.
Secondary Dominants and Tonicization (#/arts/music-theory/harmony/secondary-dominants): V of V and other borrowed dominants.
Chromatic Harmony (#/arts/music-theory/harmony/chromatic-harmony): mode mixture, the Neapolitan sixth, augmented sixth chords and common-tone diminished chords.

blocks.text: The classic keyboard exercise is to play a progression in four voices: bass in the left hand, three upper voices in the right hand, each upper voice moving to the nearest note of the next chord. Play I–IV–V7–I in every key this way; it trains your hands to find voice leading and your ear to hear function.

blocks.title: Functions
blocks.text: Label each chord's function in C major: Am, Dm7, G7, F, Bdim.
solution: Am = vi: tonic substitute. Dm7 = ii7: predominant. G7 = V7: dominant. F = IV: predominant. B° = vii°: dominant.

blocks.title: Progression
blocks.text: Write I–ii6–V7–I in D major, giving the notes of each chord and the bass note.
solution: D major: D E F♯ G A B C♯. I = D F♯ A (bass D). ii6 = E G B with G in the bass. V7 = A C♯ E G (bass A). I = D F♯ A (bass D).
blocks.answer: D–F♯–A; G (bass) E B; A C♯ E G; D F♯ A
